The **Julio Martínez Prádanos National Stadium** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Estadio Nacional Julio Martínez Prádanos_, Latin American Spanish pronunciation:[[esˈtaðjo nasjoˈnal ˈxuljo maɾˈtines ˈpɾaðanos]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium "Stadium") in [Santiago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago "Santiago"), Chile. Located in the [Ñuñoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91u%C3%B1oa "Ñuñoa") commune, it is part of the National Stadium Sports Park, a 62 [hectare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare") sporting complex which also features [tennis courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_court "Tennis court"), an aquatics center, a modern [gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gym "Gym"), a velodrome, a BMX circuit, and an assistant ground/warmup athletics track.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-Park-2)

Construction began in February 1937 and the stadium was inaugurated on 3 December 1938. The [architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture") was based on the [Olympiastadion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Stadium_(Berlin) "Olympic Stadium (Berlin)") in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), Germany. The stadium was one of the venues for the [FIFA World Cup in 1962](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_FIFA_World_Cup "1962 FIFA World Cup"), and hosted [the final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_FIFA_World_Cup_Final "1962 FIFA World Cup Final") where [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team") defeated [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia_national_football_team "Czechoslovakia national football team") 3–1. In 1948, the stadium hosted the matches of the [South American Championship of Champions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_American_Championship_of_Champions "South American Championship of Champions"), the competition that inspired the creation of the [UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-3) and of the [Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores "Copa Libertadores").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-4) The stadium was notoriously used as a [mass imprisonment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment "Internment"), [torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture_in_Chile "Torture in Chile"), and extrajudicial execution facility by the [Pinochet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_Pinochet "Augusto Pinochet") dictatorship following the [1973 military coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Chilean_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1973 Chilean coup d'état").

In 2009, a complete modernization plan was unveiled for the stadium and surrounding facilities. President [Michelle Bachelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Bachelet "Michelle Bachelet") said it would become the most modern stadium in South America.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-latercera-5) A roof above the stands was initially proposed by Bachelet in order to make the stadium an indoor venue, however, this was never completed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-6) The stadium was the opening and closing ceremonies, athletics, and football venue for the [2014 South American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_South_American_Games "2014 South American Games"), and hosted the opening ceremonies and the athletics during the [2023 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Pan_American_Games "2023 Pan American Games"). The stadium also hosted the opening ceremonies of the [2023 Parapan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Parapan_American_Games "2023 Parapan American Games").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez%2C_Estadio%2C_1954-10-02_%28594%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez,_Estadio,_1954-10-02_(594)_(cropped).jpg)

The stadium is named after journalist [Julio Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_(journalist) "Julio Martínez (journalist)") (pictured in 1952), who had an over 60 year career before his passing in 2008.

The stadium was built on former farmland, donated in 1918 by landowner and philanthropist Jose Domingo Cañas. The first sporting event in the new stadium took place on 3 December 1938, with a friendly game between the Chilean club [Colo-Colo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colo-Colo "Colo-Colo") and Brazilian club [São Cristóvão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Crist%C3%B3v%C3%A3o_de_Futebol_e_Regatas "São Cristóvão de Futebol e Regatas"), with the former winning 6–3.

It has hosted all matches of the [1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1941_South_American_Championship "1941 South American Championship"), [1945](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1945_South_American_Championship "1945 South American Championship") and [1955](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_South_American_Championship "1955 South American Championship") South American Football Championships, and several matches of the [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Copa_Am%C3%A9rica "1991 Copa América") and [2015 Copa América](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Copa_Am%C3%A9rica "2015 Copa América").

The stadium hosted the final stages of the [1959 World Basketball Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_FIBA_World_Championship "1959 FIBA World Championship"). It was held outdoors because the intended venue, the [Metropolitan Indoor Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movistar_Arena_(Santiago) "Movistar Arena (Santiago)"), was not ready in time.

In the early 1960s, under the government of [Jorge Alessandri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Alessandri "Jorge Alessandri"), the stadium was expanded to host the [1962 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_FIFA_World_Cup "1962 FIFA World Cup"). The main modification was replacing the velodrome that surrounded the stadium with galleries, thereby increasing its capacity to around 95,000.

The stadium hosted group stage games between [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_national_football_team "Germany national football team"), [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_national_football_team "Switzerland national football team") and Chile, including a notoriously ill-tempered and violent clash between Italy and Chile which became known as the [Battle of Santiago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Santiago_(1962_FIFA_World_Cup) "Battle of Santiago (1962 FIFA World Cup)"). A quarter-final, a semi-final, the third place play-off, and the final were also held at the ground, where Brazil was crowned world champions for the second time. In the third-place play-off, Chile defeated [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia_national_football_team "Yugoslavia national football team") 1–0, marking the team's greatest success in international football.

Today, the ground serves as the home field for both the national team and the first-division club [Universidad de Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_Chile_(football_club) "Universidad de Chile (football club)"). It also hosts non-sporting events, such as political celebrations, charity events and concerts.

The stadium had been used since 1995 as the final leg of the [Teletón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telet%C3%B3n_(Chile) "Teletón (Chile)") with [Don Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Francisco_(television_host) "Don Francisco (television host)"), a 28-hour telecast. The stadium holds up to 100,000 people for this annual event with the Jumbotron showing the required amount required to reach the goal and the current donation level. Exceptions were in 2014 and 2020; the first one was canceled due to bad weather conditions and the second due to the protection after [the social outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019-20_Chilean_protests "2019-20 Chilean protests").

On 5 July 2008, the stadium was officially renamed **Estadio Nacional Julio Martínez Prádanos**, in honor of [Julio Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_(journalist) "Julio Martínez (journalist)"), a Chilean sports commentator specializing in football who had a long career in the written press, radio and television, who had died in January of the same year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-7)

### Use as a detention center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Use as a detention center")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Chile-_el_pueblo_vencera_cropped.jpg/250px-Chile-_el_pueblo_vencera_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chile-_el_pueblo_vencera_cropped.jpg)

Military units watching over prisioners detained at the stadium, 1973.

After the [coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Chilean_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1973 Chilean coup d'état") of 11 September 1973, that ousted President [Salvador Allende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Allende "Salvador Allende"), the stadium began to be used as a detention facility. An article in the _Harvard Review of Latin America_ reported that "there were over 80 detention centers in Santiago alone" and gave details of the National Stadium and others.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-8)

Between 12,000 and 20,000 people spent time in the compound during the _junta_ regime. Twelve thousand detainees were interned between 11 September and 7 November.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-9) The field and gallery were used to hold men, while women were held in the [swimming pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_pool "Swimming pool") changing rooms and associated buildings. Locker rooms and corridors were all used as prison facilities while interrogations were carried out in the [velodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velodrome "Velodrome").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-10) The Red Cross estimated that 7,000 prisoners occupied the stadium at one point, of whom about 300 were foreigners. According to the testimonies of survivors collected by the humanitarian group, detainees were tortured and threatened with death by shooting. Some were actually shot or taken to unknown locations for execution.

[FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA") President [Sir Stanley Rous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Rous "Stanley Rous") insisted the [USSR team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR_national_football_team "USSR national football team") play [a World Cup qualifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification_(UEFA%E2%80%93CONMEBOL_play-off) "1974 FIFA World Cup qualification (UEFA–CONMEBOL play-off)") at the time. They however refused to do so and [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile_national_football_team "Chile national football team") qualified automatically for the [1974 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup "1974 FIFA World Cup"), where they failed to advance from a group containing both [West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_national_football_team "German national football team") and [East Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany_national_football_team "East Germany national football team") and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_men's_national_soccer_team "Australia men's national soccer team").

The use of the stadium during the coup d'état is depicted in the 2002 [documentary film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_film "Documentary film")_Estadio Nacional_, directed and produced by [Carmen Luz Parot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_Luz_Parot "Carmen Luz Parot"), and in the 2007 Swedish film _[The Black Pimpernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Pimpernel "The Black Pimpernel")_, which is based on the story of Swedish ambassador in Chile [Harald Edelstam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Edelstam "Harald Edelstam") and his heroic actions to protect the lives of over 1,200 people during and after the military coup. _The Black Pimpernel_ was shot on location in Santiago. The 1982 film _[Missing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing\_(1982\_film) "Missing (1982 film)")_ by Greek filmmaker [Costa-Gavras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa-Gavras "Costa-Gavras") depicts the 11 September 1973, coup d'état and execution of American journalists [Charles Horman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Horman "Charles Horman") and [Frank Teruggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Teruggi "Frank Teruggi") at the Estadio Nacional.

In 2011, Chile set aside a section of the stadium, a section of old wooden bleachers called [Escotilla n.º 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escotilla_n.%C2%BA_8?action=edit&redlink=1 "Escotilla n.º 8 (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escotilla%20n.%C2%BA%208 "es:Escotilla n.º 8")], to honor the prisoners who were detained there. It is surrounded by a barbed wire fence.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-11)

### 2009–2010 renovation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2009–2010 renovation")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Adios_Matador.jpg/250px-Adios_Matador.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Adios_Matador.jpg)

[Marcelo Salas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelo_Salas "Marcelo Salas") farewell match, June 2, 2009

On 15 June 2009, President [Michelle Bachelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Bachelet "Michelle Bachelet") announced several infrastructure improvements in order to modernize the stadium and its immediate facilities. Out of the total 24 billion [pesos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_peso "Chilean peso") (US$42.3 million) contemplated in the plan, 20 billion pesos (US$35.3 million) are destined to bring the stadium up to modern standards. The changes include, a roof covering all the seats, which will also provide illumination; installation of seats around the entire stadium, lowering the current capacity to 47,000; a new state-of-the-art [scoreboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoreboard "Scoreboard"); a 2.5 m deep 2 m wide pit will separate the track and the spectators to replace the fence; and several other changes. Because the stadium is a [national monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Monuments_of_Chile "National Monuments of Chile") the façade will remain the same, with the roof structure placed on top, without modifying the exterior. The stadium was closed on August 15, 2009. The stadium was scheduled to be reinaugurated in March 2010 to stage a double friendly match between Chile and [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea") and [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), but the works were not finished on time. The construction of the roof has since been postponed by the government of President [Sebastián Piñera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era "Sebastián Piñera") due to financial constraints brought about by the [27 February 2010 earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Chile_earthquake "2010 Chile earthquake"). Although the stadium suffered minor damage from the earthquake, it partially opened to host the match between [C.F. Universidad de Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_Chile_(football_club) "Universidad de Chile (football club)") and [C.D. Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C.D._Guadalajara "C.D. Guadalajara") for [Copa Libertadores 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Copa_Libertadores "2010 Copa Libertadores"). It was officially re-inaugurated on 12 September 2010, during Chile's bicentennial festivities.

### 2014 South American Games renovation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2014 South American Games renovation")]

On 12 September 2010, during the Chilean bicentennial festivities, President [Sebastián Piñera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era "Sebastián Piñera") announced that the capacity of the stadium will be increased so as to reach 70,000 seats for the [2014 South American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_South_American_Games "2014 South American Games") that took place in Santiago.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-12) The works started in 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-13)

On 3 June 2011, further renovation plans were announced by the government. The complete area surrounding the stadium will be turned into a park to be called "Citizenry Park" (_Parque de la Ciudadanía_). Over 70% of the new 64-hectare park will consist of green areas, and the rest will include new infrastructure such as a lagoon or restaurants. The park was expected to be ready for the 2014 games. New sporting venues were built for the 2014 games, such as two modern gymnasiums, a new heated pool for [synchronized swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronized_swimming "Synchronized swimming"), a renovated velodrome and an expanded CAR, which will also serve as residence of the future Ministry of Sports. The only venues that will remain are the stadium, the main tennis court, the velodrome, the CAR, the athletics track, the skating track, the hockey field and the _caracolas_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-14)

## Attendances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Attendances")]

The highest attendance for a match at Estadio Nacional to date is 85,268, for a [Primera Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liga_Chilena_de_F%C3%BAtbol:_Primera_Divisi%C3%B3n "Liga Chilena de Fútbol: Primera División") match played on 29 December 1962; [Universidad de Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_Chile_(football_club) "Universidad de Chile (football club)") defeated [Universidad Catolica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Deportivo_Universidad_Cat%C3%B3lica "Club Deportivo Universidad Católica") 4–1.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In the 2016–17 season, [Universidad de Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_Chile "Universidad de Chile") drew an average home league attendance of 30,041 for the Apertura and 33,466 for the Clausura.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-17)

## Concerts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Concerts")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Sticky_And_Sweet_Tour_2008_Santiago_Chile.JPG/330px-Sticky_And_Sweet_Tour_2008_Santiago_Chile.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sticky_And_Sweet_Tour_2008_Santiago_Chile.JPG)

In 2008, [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna "Madonna") was the first international artist to perform two concerts in two consecutive days in the stadium since 1990. Pictured, the second show of her [Sticky & Sweet Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_&_Sweet_Tour "Sticky & Sweet Tour") in the venue.

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/U2_360%C2%B0_Tour_en_Chile_1.jpg/330px-U2_360%C2%B0_Tour_en_Chile_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U2_360%C2%B0_Tour_en_Chile_1.jpg)

The [U2 360° Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2_360%C2%B0_Tour "U2 360° Tour") became the biggest stage structure built inside the stadium to date.

The stadium hosts many international and national concerts during the year. In 1977, Spanish singer [Julio Iglesias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Iglesias "Julio Iglesias") was the first musical act and first solo artist to perform in the stadium.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-Julio77-18) Years later, in 1989, [Rod Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Stewart "Rod Stewart") performed what is considered the first proper rock concert by an international artist in the venue, drawing 70,000 fans to his [Out of Order Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_Order_Tour "Out of Order Tour"), with the show being broadcast on TV throughout the country.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-19) After that show, the city started being included in many tours from international artists, using several facilities from the Stadium park.

In 2001, Chilean band [Los Prisioneros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Prisioneros "Los Prisioneros") became the first act to perform two consecutive days in the stadium, while [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna "Madonna") is considered the first international artist to achieve the same in 2008. In 2022, Puerto Rican star [Daddy Yankee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daddy_Yankee "Daddy Yankee") became the first act to sell out three concerts in the venue on a single day,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-20) while British band [Coldplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coldplay "Coldplay") became the first act to schedule three and four consecutive concerts as part of the same tour.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-22) In 2023, Chilean band [Los Bunkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Bunkers "Los Bunkers") became the second Chilean act to book two consecutive concerts in the venue, after Los Prisioneros achieved the same in 2001.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-23) In 2024, Colombian singer [Karol G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_G "Karol G") became the first solo female act to sell out three consecutive concerts in the venue.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-24) In 2025, Chilean singer [Myriam Hernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_Hern%C3%A1ndez "Myriam Hernández") became the first Chilean solo female act to book a concert in the venue.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-25)

Recordings of concerts at the stadium have been commercially released. The show of Cuban folk singer [Silvio Rodríguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvio_Rodr%C3%ADguez "Silvio Rodríguez") in March 1990 was released on a 2CD set titled _Silvio Rodríguez en Chile_, while both concerts of [Los Prisioneros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Prisioneros "Los Prisioneros") in late 2001 were released on cassette and CD as _Estadio Nacional_, and on VHS and DVD as _Lo Estamos Pasando Muy Bien_. English heavy metal band [Iron Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Maiden "Iron Maiden") recorded their show in the venue during [The Final Frontier World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Final_Frontier_World_Tour "The Final Frontier World Tour") in April 2011. The show was released on CD, LP, DVD and Blu-ray as _[En Vivo!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En\_Vivo!\_(Iron\_Maiden\_album) "En Vivo! (Iron Maiden album)")_ in March 2012.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-SA_&_Germany-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-En_Vivo!_main-27)

## Capacity

The stadium was built with an original capacity of 48,000 spectators in 1937. At the time, some considered it a "[white elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_elephant "White elephant")" because it was thought that it could never be filled. The term also alluded to the charges of corruption against the administration of [Arturo Alessandri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Alessandri "Arturo Alessandri"), which oversaw the stadium's costly construction.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-59)

For the [1962 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_FIFA_World_Cup "1962 FIFA World Cup"), seating capacity was increased to 74,000 with overflow areas allowing for a total of more than 80,000 people, by eliminating the cycling track that was moved to another location. Over the years, seating capacity was reduced to keep escape routes clear and prevent accidents.

For the [2000 World Junior Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2000 World Junior Championships in Athletics"), the installation of individual seats was required, which reduced capacity to 66,000 spectators. The **Julio Martínez Prádanos National Stadium** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Estadio Nacional Julio Martínez Prádanos_, Latin American Spanish pronunciation:[[esˈtaðjo nasjoˈnal ˈxuljo maɾˈtines ˈpɾaðanos]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium "Stadium") in [Santiago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago "Santiago"), Chile. Located in the [Ñuñoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91u%C3%B1oa "Ñuñoa") commune, it is part of the National Stadium Sports Park, a 62 [hectare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare") sporting complex which also features [tennis courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_court "Tennis court"), an aquatics center, a modern [gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gym "Gym"), a velodrome, a BMX circuit, and an assistant ground/warmup athletics track.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-Park-2)

Construction began in February 1937 and the stadium was inaugurated on 3 December 1938. The [architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture") was based on the [Olympiastadion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Stadium_(Berlin) "Olympic Stadium (Berlin)") in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), Germany. The stadium was one of the venues for the [FIFA World Cup in 1962](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_FIFA_World_Cup "1962 FIFA World Cup"), and hosted [the final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_FIFA_World_Cup_Final "1962 FIFA World Cup Final") where [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team") defeated [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia_national_football_team "Czechoslovakia national football team") 3–1. In 1948, the stadium hosted the matches of the [South American Championship of Champions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_American_Championship_of_Champions "South American Championship of Champions"), the competition that inspired the creation of the [UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-3) and of the [Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores "Copa Libertadores").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-4) The stadium was notoriously used as a [mass imprisonment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment "Internment"), [torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture_in_Chile "Torture in Chile"), and extrajudicial execution facility by the [Pinochet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_Pinochet "Augusto Pinochet") dictatorship following the [1973 military coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Chilean_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1973 Chilean coup d'état").

In 2009, a complete modernization plan was unveiled for the stadium and surrounding facilities. President [Michelle Bachelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Bachelet "Michelle Bachelet") said it would become the most modern stadium in South America.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-latercera-5) A roof above the stands was initially proposed by Bachelet in order to make the stadium an indoor venue, however, this was never completed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-6) The stadium was the opening and closing ceremonies, athletics, and football venue for the [2014 South American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_South_American_Games "2014 South American Games"), and hosted the opening ceremonies and the athletics during the [2023 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Pan_American_Games "2023 Pan American Games"). The stadium also hosted the opening ceremonies of the [2023 Parapan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Parapan_American_Games "2023 Parapan American Games").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez%2C_Estadio%2C_1954-10-02_%28594%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez,_Estadio,_1954-10-02_(594)_(cropped).jpg)

The stadium is named after journalist [Julio Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_(journalist) "Julio Martínez (journalist)") (pictured in 1952), who had an over 60 year career before his passing in 2008.

The stadium was built on former farmland, donated in 1918 by landowner and philanthropist Jose Domingo Cañas. The first sporting event in the new stadium took place on 3 December 1938, with a friendly game between the Chilean club [Colo-Colo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colo-Colo "Colo-Colo") and Brazilian club [São Cristóvão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Crist%C3%B3v%C3%A3o_de_Futebol_e_Regatas "São Cristóvão de Futebol e Regatas"), with the former winning 6–3.

It has hosted all matches of the [1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1941_South_American_Championship "1941 South American Championship"), [1945](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1945_South_American_Championship "1945 South American Championship") and [1955](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_South_American_Championship "1955 South American Championship") South American Football Championships, and several matches of the [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Copa_Am%C3%A9rica "1991 Copa América") and [2015 Copa América](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Copa_Am%C3%A9rica "2015 Copa América").

The stadium hosted the final stages of the [1959 World Basketball Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_FIBA_World_Championship "1959 FIBA World Championship"). It was held outdoors because the intended venue, the [Metropolitan Indoor Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movistar_Arena_(Santiago) "Movistar Arena (Santiago)"), was not ready in time.

In the early 1960s, under the government of [Jorge Alessandri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Alessandri "Jorge Alessandri"), the stadium was expanded to host the [1962 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_FIFA_World_Cup "1962 FIFA World Cup"). The main modification was replacing the velodrome that surrounded the stadium with galleries, thereby increasing its capacity to around 95,000.

The stadium hosted group stage games between [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_national_football_team "Germany national football team"), [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_national_football_team "Switzerland national football team") and Chile, including a notoriously ill-tempered and violent clash between Italy and Chile which became known as the [Battle of Santiago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Santiago_(1962_FIFA_World_Cup) "Battle of Santiago (1962 FIFA World Cup)"). A quarter-final, a semi-final, the third place play-off, and the final were also held at the ground, where Brazil was crowned world champions for the second time. In the third-place play-off, Chile defeated [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia_national_football_team "Yugoslavia national football team") 1–0, marking the team's greatest success in international football.

Today, the ground serves as the home field for both the national team and the first-division club [Universidad de Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_Chile_(football_club) "Universidad de Chile (football club)"). It also hosts non-sporting events, such as political celebrations, charity events and concerts.

The stadium had been used since 1995 as the final leg of the [Teletón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telet%C3%B3n_(Chile) "Teletón (Chile)") with [Don Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Francisco_(television_host) "Don Francisco (television host)"), a 28-hour telecast. The stadium holds up to 100,000 people for this annual event with the Jumbotron showing the required amount required to reach the goal and the current donation level. Exceptions were in 2014 and 2020; the first one was canceled due to bad weather conditions and the second due to the protection after [the social outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019-20_Chilean_protests "2019-20 Chilean protests").

On 5 July 2008, the stadium was officially renamed **Estadio Nacional Julio Martínez Prádanos**, in honor of [Julio Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_(journalist) "Julio Martínez (journalist)"), a Chilean sports commentator specializing in football who had a long career in the written press, radio and television, who had died in January of the same year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-7)

### Use as a detention center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Use as a detention center")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Chile-_el_pueblo_vencera_cropped.jpg/250px-Chile-_el_pueblo_vencera_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chile-_el_pueblo_vencera_cropped.jpg)

Military units watching over prisioners detained at the stadium, 1973.

After the [coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Chilean_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1973 Chilean coup d'état") of 11 September 1973, that ousted President [Salvador Allende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Allende "Salvador Allende"), the stadium began to be used as a detention facility. An article in the _Harvard Review of Latin America_ reported that "there were over 80 detention centers in Santiago alone" and gave details of the National Stadium and others.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-8)

Between 12,000 and 20,000 people spent time in the compound during the _junta_ regime. Twelve thousand detainees were interned between 11 September and 7 November.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-9) The field and gallery were used to hold men, while women were held in the [swimming pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_pool "Swimming pool") changing rooms and associated buildings. Locker rooms and corridors were all used as prison facilities while interrogations were carried out in the [velodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velodrome "Velodrome").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-10) The Red Cross estimated that 7,000 prisoners occupied the stadium at one point, of whom about 300 were foreigners. According to the testimonies of survivors collected by the humanitarian group, detainees were tortured and threatened with death by shooting. Some were actually shot or taken to unknown locations for execution.

[FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA") President [Sir Stanley Rous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Rous "Stanley Rous") insisted the [USSR team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR_national_football_team "USSR national football team") play [a World Cup qualifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification_(UEFA%E2%80%93CONMEBOL_play-off) "1974 FIFA World Cup qualification (UEFA–CONMEBOL play-off)") at the time. They however refused to do so and [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile_national_football_team "Chile national football team") qualified automatically for the [1974 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup "1974 FIFA World Cup"), where they failed to advance from a group containing both [West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_national_football_team "German national football team") and [East Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany_national_football_team "East Germany national football team") and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_men's_national_soccer_team "Australia men's national soccer team").

The use of the stadium during the coup d'état is depicted in the 2002 [documentary film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_film "Documentary film")_Estadio Nacional_, directed and produced by [Carmen Luz Parot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_Luz_Parot "Carmen Luz Parot"), and in the 2007 Swedish film _[The Black Pimpernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Pimpernel "The Black Pimpernel")_, which is based on the story of Swedish ambassador in Chile [Harald Edelstam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Edelstam "Harald Edelstam") and his heroic actions to protect the lives of over 1,200 people during and after the military coup. _The Black Pimpernel_ was shot on location in Santiago. The 1982 film _[Missing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing\_(1982\_film) "Missing (1982 film)")_ by Greek filmmaker [Costa-Gavras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa-Gavras "Costa-Gavras") depicts the 11 September 1973, coup d'état and execution of American journalists [Charles Horman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Horman "Charles Horman") and [Frank Teruggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Teruggi "Frank Teruggi") at the Estadio Nacional.

In 2011, Chile set aside a section of the stadium, a section of old wooden bleachers called [Escotilla n.º 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escotilla_n.%C2%BA_8?action=edit&redlink=1 "Escotilla n.º 8 (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escotilla%20n.%C2%BA%208 "es:Escotilla n.º 8")], to honor the prisoners who were detained there. It is surrounded by a barbed wire fence.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-11)

### 2009–2010 renovation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2009–2010 renovation")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Adios_Matador.jpg/250px-Adios_Matador.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Adios_Matador.jpg)

[Marcelo Salas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelo_Salas "Marcelo Salas") farewell match, June 2, 2009

On 15 June 2009, President [Michelle Bachelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Bachelet "Michelle Bachelet") announced several infrastructure improvements in order to modernize the stadium and its immediate facilities. Out of the total 24 billion [pesos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_peso "Chilean peso") (US$42.3 million) contemplated in the plan, 20 billion pesos (US$35.3 million) are destined to bring the stadium up to modern standards. The changes include, a roof covering all the seats, which will also provide illumination; installation of seats around the entire stadium, lowering the current capacity to 47,000; a new state-of-the-art [scoreboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoreboard "Scoreboard"); a 2.5 m deep 2 m wide pit will separate the track and the spectators to replace the fence; and several other changes. Because the stadium is a [national monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Monuments_of_Chile "National Monuments of Chile") the façade will remain the same, with the roof structure placed on top, without modifying the exterior. The stadium was closed on August 15, 2009. The stadium was scheduled to be reinaugurated in March 2010 to stage a double friendly match between Chile and [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea") and [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), but the works were not finished on time. The construction of the roof has since been postponed by the government of President [Sebastián Piñera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era "Sebastián Piñera") due to financial constraints brought about by the [27 February 2010 earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Chile_earthquake "2010 Chile earthquake"). Although the stadium suffered minor damage from the earthquake, it partially opened to host the match between [C.F. Universidad de Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_Chile_(football_club) "Universidad de Chile (football club)") and [C.D. Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C.D._Guadalajara "C.D. Guadalajara") for [Copa Libertadores 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Copa_Libertadores "2010 Copa Libertadores"). It was officially re-inaugurated on 12 September 2010, during Chile's bicentennial festivities.

### 2014 South American Games renovation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2014 South American Games renovation")]

On 12 September 2010, during the Chilean bicentennial festivities, President [Sebastián Piñera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era "Sebastián Piñera") announced that the capacity of the stadium will be increased so as to reach 70,000 seats for the [2014 South American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_South_American_Games "2014 South American Games") that took place in Santiago.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-12) The works started in 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-13)

On 3 June 2011, further renovation plans were announced by the government. The complete area surrounding the stadium will be turned into a park to be called "Citizenry Park" (_Parque de la Ciudadanía_). Over 70% of the new 64-hectare park will consist of green areas, and the rest will include new infrastructure such as a lagoon or restaurants. The park was expected to be ready for the 2014 games. New sporting venues were built for the 2014 games, such as two modern gymnasiums, a new heated pool for [synchronized swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronized_swimming "Synchronized swimming"), a renovated velodrome and an expanded CAR, which will also serve as residence of the future Ministry of Sports. The only venues that will remain are the stadium, the main tennis court, the velodrome, the CAR, the athletics track, the skating track, the hockey field and the _caracolas_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-14)

## Concerts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Julio_Mart%C3%ADnez_Pr%C3%A1danos_National_Stadium&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Concerts")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Sticky_And_Sweet_Tour_2008_Santiago_Chile.JPG/330px-Sticky_And_Sweet_Tour_2008_Santiago_Chile.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sticky_And_Sweet_Tour_2008_Santiago_Chile.JPG)

In 2008, [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna "Madonna") was the first international artist to perform two concerts in two consecutive days in the stadium since 1990. Pictured, the second show of her [Sticky & Sweet Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_&_Sweet_Tour "Sticky & Sweet Tour") in the venue.

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/U2_360%C2%B0_Tour_en_Chile_1.jpg/330px-U2_360%C2%B0_Tour_en_Chile_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U2_360%C2%B0_Tour_en_Chile_1.jpg)

The [U2 360° Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2_360%C2%B0_Tour "U2 360° Tour") became the biggest stage structure built inside the stadium to date.

The stadium hosts many international and national concerts during the year. In 1977, Spanish singer [Julio Iglesias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Iglesias "Julio Iglesias") was the first musical act and first solo artist to perform in the stadium.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-Julio77-18) Years later, in 1989, [Rod Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Stewart "Rod Stewart") performed what is considered the first proper rock concert by an international artist in the venue, drawing 70,000 fans to his [Out of Order Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_Order_Tour "Out of Order Tour"), with the show being broadcast on TV throughout the country.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-19) After that show, the city started being included in many tours from international artists, using several facilities from the Stadium park.

In 2001, Chilean band [Los Prisioneros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Prisioneros "Los Prisioneros") became the first act to perform two consecutive days in the stadium, while [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna "Madonna") is considered the first international artist to achieve the same in 2008. In 2022, Puerto Rican star [Daddy Yankee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daddy_Yankee "Daddy Yankee") became the first act to sell out three concerts in the venue on a single day,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-20) while British band [Coldplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coldplay "Coldplay") became the first act to schedule three and four consecutive concerts as part of the same tour.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-22) In 2023, Chilean band [Los Bunkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Bunkers "Los Bunkers") became the second Chilean act to book two consecutive concerts in the venue, after Los Prisioneros achieved the same in 2001.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-23) In 2024, Colombian singer [Karol G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_G "Karol G") became the first solo female act to sell out three consecutive concerts in the venue.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-24) In 2025, Chilean singer [Myriam Hernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_Hern%C3%A1ndez "Myriam Hernández") became the first Chilean solo female act to book a concert in the venue.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-25)

Recordings of concerts at the stadium have been commercially released. The show of Cuban folk singer [Silvio Rodríguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvio_Rodr%C3%ADguez "Silvio Rodríguez") in March 1990 was released on a 2CD set titled _Silvio Rodríguez en Chile_, while both concerts of [Los Prisioneros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Prisioneros "Los Prisioneros") in late 2001 were released on cassette and CD as _Estadio Nacional_, and on VHS and DVD as _Lo Estamos Pasando Muy Bien_. English heavy metal band [Iron Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Maiden "Iron Maiden") recorded their show in the venue during [The Final Frontier World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Final_Frontier_World_Tour "The Final Frontier World Tour") in April 2011. The show was released on CD, LP, DVD and Blu-ray as _[En Vivo!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En\_Vivo!\_(Iron\_Maiden\_album) "En Vivo! (Iron Maiden album)")_ in March 2012.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-SA_&_Germany-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Nacional_(Chile)#cite_note-En_Vivo!_main-27)

The **2004 UEFA Champions League final** was an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") match played on 26 May 2004 to decide the winner of the [2003–04 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003%E2%80%9304_UEFA_Champions_League "2003–04 UEFA Champions League"). [AS Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AS_Monaco_FC "AS Monaco FC"), a [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco")-based club representing the [French Football Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Football_Federation "French Football Federation"), faced Portuguese side [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Porto "FC Porto") at the [Arena AufSchalke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_AufSchalke "Arena AufSchalke") in [Gelsenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelsenkirchen "Gelsenkirchen"), Germany. Porto won the match 3–0, with [Carlos Alberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Alberto_de_Jesus "Carlos Alberto de Jesus"), [Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deco "Deco") and [Dmitri Alenichev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Alenichev "Dmitri Alenichev") scoring the goals in a dominant game from Jose Mourinho's Porto. Deco was named Man of the Match.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/F.C._Porto_Museum_11.jpg/250px-F.C._Porto_Museum_11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:F.C._Porto_Museum_11.jpg)

The UEFA Champions League trophy is on display at the FC Porto Museum in [Estádio do Dragão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A1dio_do_Drag%C3%A3o "Estádio do Dragão").

Porto's previous triumph in the competition had been in [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_European_Cup_final "1987 European Cup final") – although they had won the [UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") in the [previous season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002%E2%80%9303_UEFA_Cup "2002–03 UEFA Cup") – while Monaco were playing in their first ever UEFA Champions League final. Both teams started their campaigns in the group stage and defeated former European champions on their way to the final: Porto beat 1968 and 1999 winners [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") while Monaco defeated nine-time champions [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF").

Both teams were considered [underdogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underdog_(competition) "Underdog (competition)") in the competition before reaching the final stages and were led by young managers. Monaco had hired former [France national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team") captain [Didier Deschamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Deschamps "Didier Deschamps") as manager and Porto were led by rising star [José Mourinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Mourinho "José Mourinho"), who left the club for [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") a week after the match.

Monaco became the fourth club representing the [French league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligue_1 "Ligue 1") to reach the final after [Reims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_de_Reims "Stade de Reims") in [1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_European_Cup_final "1956 European Cup final")&[1959](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_European_Cup_final "1959 European Cup final"), [Saint-Étienne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AS_Saint-%C3%89tienne "AS Saint-Étienne") in [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_European_Cup_final "1976 European Cup final"), and [Olympique de Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_de_Marseille "Olympique de Marseille") in [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_European_Cup_final "1991 European Cup final")&[1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1993 UEFA Champions League final"). This was the fifth final in the history of the European Cup in which neither of the teams came from England, Germany, Italy or Spain and the first since the 1991 final when [Red Star Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Star_Belgrade "Red Star Belgrade") of Yugoslavia beat Marseille. To date, this is the last Champions League final to feature a team from outside the [Big Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Five_(association_football) "Big Five (association football)") European leagues (England, France, Germany, Italy, Spain), and the last one to be won by a team from outside those five leagues.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-2)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

### Monaco

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Monaco")]

Monaco finished second in the French [Ligue 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligue_1 "Ligue 1") the previous season, meaning that they entered the Champions League at the group stage. Monaco were placed in Group C, alongside [Deportivo La Coruña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportivo_de_La_Coru%C3%B1a "Deportivo de La Coruña"), [PSV Eindhoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSV_Eindhoven "PSV Eindhoven") and [AEK Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEK_Athens_F.C. "AEK Athens F.C."). After a 2–1 in their first win in the Netherlands and a 4–0 win at the [Stade Louis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_Louis_II "Stade Louis II") against AEK Athens, Monaco travelled to Spain, losing 1–0 by Deportivo. The Monegasque adventure really began after the return match against Deportivo, when Monaco won 8–3, which represented the highest number of goals in one match in the history of the new version of the UEFA Champions League; this record lasted until 22 November 2016, when [Legia Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legia_Warsaw "Legia Warsaw") lost 8–4 to [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"). Croatian striker [Dado Pršo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dado_Pr%C5%A1o "Dado Pršo") scored four times, while captain [Ludovic Giuly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Giuly "Ludovic Giuly") (2), [Jérôme Rothen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A9r%C3%B4me_Rothen "Jérôme Rothen"), [Jaroslav Plašil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaroslav_Pla%C5%A1il "Jaroslav Plašil") and [Édouard Cissé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Ciss%C3%A9 "Édouard Cissé") pulverised the Spanish defensive line. After two more draws against PSV and AEK Athens, Monaco finished at the top of Group C.

The first knockout round saw Monaco winning against [Lokomotiv Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Lokomotiv_Moscow "FC Lokomotiv Moscow") after a 2–1 defeat in Russia and a win 1–0 at Stade Louis II. In the quarter-finals, Monaco played [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF"). After a 4–2 loss in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") (where [Fernando Morientes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Morientes "Fernando Morientes") scored, and was applauded by his former fans), Monaco created a sensation by defeating the Spanish 3–1 at home. Monaco played against [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") in the semi-finals, and despite the exclusion of [Akis Zikos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akis_Zikos "Akis Zikos"), Monaco found enough strength to score twice and win the game 3–1.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-3) The last goal was scored by striker [Shabani Nonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabani_Nonda "Shabani Nonda"), who just returned from a seven-month injury. The second leg at [Stamford Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamford_Bridge_(stadium) "Stamford Bridge (stadium)") saw Monaco resisting Chelsea's strikes, for a final score of 2–2 to reach the European Cup final for the first time in their history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bbcsport-4)

### Porto

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Porto")]

Porto, winners of the [Primeira Liga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primeira_Liga "Primeira Liga"), [Taça de Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C3%A7a_de_Portugal "Taça de Portugal") and [UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") in 2002–03, were the only Portuguese team in the group stage, after the elimination of [Benfica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S.L._Benfica "S.L. Benfica") in the third qualifying round by Italian side [Lazio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Lazio "SS Lazio"). Porto was drawn in Group F, along with Real Madrid, [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_de_Marseille "Olympique de Marseille") and [Partizan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK_Partizan "FK Partizan"). Porto's first match was at [Partizan Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partizan_Stadium "Partizan Stadium") in [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade"). [Costinha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costinha "Costinha") scored the opening goal on 22 minutes, but [Andrija Delibašić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrija_Deliba%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Andrija Delibašić") scored the equaliser on 54 minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-5) The next match, the first at the [Estádio das Antas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A1dio_das_Antas "Estádio das Antas"), was a 3–1 loss to Real Madrid. Costinha scored the opening goal again, on seven minutes. [Iván Helguera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iv%C3%A1n_Helguera "Iván Helguera") equalised on 28 minutes; [Santiago Solari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Solari "Santiago Solari") on 37 minutes and [Zinedine Zidane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinedine_Zidane "Zinedine Zidane") on 67 scored Real Madrid's winning goals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-6)

Two straight wins against Marseille followed by a win at home against Partizan secured Porto's place in the first knockout round before the last match of the group stage, a draw in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-7) In the first knockout round, Porto met [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C."). The Portuguese won 2–1 at home[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-8) and managed to qualify in the final minutes of the second leg, when Costinha scored an equaliser in [injury time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football#Duration_and_tie-breaking_methods "Association football") in a 1–1 draw at [Old Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Trafford "Old Trafford").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-9) In the quarter-finals, Porto met a French team for the second time in the tournament: a 2–0 win at home[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-10) and a 2–2 draw in France eliminated [Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_Lyonnais "Olympique Lyonnais") from the competition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-11) In the semi-finals, Porto played Deportivo La Coruña, eliminating them 1–0 on aggregate.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-12)

## Match

### Summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Summary")]

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/FCP-CL_Supporters.jpg/250px-FCP-CL_Supporters.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FCP-CL_Supporters.jpg)

FC Porto supporters at the Gelsenkirchen Arena AufSchalke.

Monaco, in their first European final since the 1992 Europa Cup,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bbcsport-4) were up against Porto, the UEFA Cup winners from the previous season,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bbcsport-4) who were appearing in the European Cup final for a second time, after defeating [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") in the [1987 European Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_European_Cup_final "1987 European Cup final").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-uefareport-13) Porto were the favourites after eliminating Manchester United and Deportivo La Coruña in the knockout phase, while Monaco had eliminated Real Madrid and Chelsea.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Porto won the match 3–0; [Carlos Alberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Alberto_(footballer,_born_December_1984) "Carlos Alberto (footballer, born December 1984)") opened the scoring in the first half, while [Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deco "Deco") and [Dmitri Alenichev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Alenichev "Dmitri Alenichev") extended Porto's lead in the second half.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-14)

The **2004 UEFA Champions League final** was an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") match played on 26 May 2004 to decide the winner of the [2003–04 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003%E2%80%9304_UEFA_Champions_League "2003–04 UEFA Champions League"). [AS Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AS_Monaco_FC "AS Monaco FC"), a [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco")-based club representing the [French Football Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Football_Federation "French Football Federation"), faced Portuguese side [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Porto "FC Porto") at the [Arena AufSchalke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_AufSchalke "Arena AufSchalke") in [Gelsenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelsenkirchen "Gelsenkirchen"), Germany. Porto won the match 3–0, with [Carlos Alberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Alberto_de_Jesus "Carlos Alberto de Jesus"), [Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deco "Deco") and [Dmitri Alenichev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Alenichev "Dmitri Alenichev") scoring the goals in a dominant game from Jose Mourinho's Porto. Deco was named Man of the Match.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/F.C._Porto_Museum_11.jpg/250px-F.C._Porto_Museum_11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:F.C._Porto_Museum_11.jpg)

The UEFA Champions League trophy is on display at the FC Porto Museum in [Estádio do Dragão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A1dio_do_Drag%C3%A3o "Estádio do Dragão").

Porto's previous triumph in the competition had been in [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_European_Cup_final "1987 European Cup final") – although they had won the [UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") in the [previous season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002%E2%80%9303_UEFA_Cup "2002–03 UEFA Cup") – while Monaco were playing in their first ever UEFA Champions League final. Both teams started their campaigns in the group stage and defeated former European champions on their way to the final: Porto beat 1968 and 1999 winners [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") while Monaco defeated nine-time champions [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF").

Both teams were considered [underdogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underdog_(competition) "Underdog (competition)") in the competition before reaching the final stages and were led by young managers. Monaco had hired former [France national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team") captain [Didier Deschamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Deschamps "Didier Deschamps") as manager and Porto were led by rising star [José Mourinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Mourinho "José Mourinho"), who left the club for [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") a week after the match.

Monaco became the fourth club representing the [French league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligue_1 "Ligue 1") to reach the final after [Reims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_de_Reims "Stade de Reims") in [1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_European_Cup_final "1956 European Cup final")&[1959](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_European_Cup_final "1959 European Cup final"), [Saint-Étienne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AS_Saint-%C3%89tienne "AS Saint-Étienne") in [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_European_Cup_final "1976 European Cup final"), and [Olympique de Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_de_Marseille "Olympique de Marseille") in [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_European_Cup_final "1991 European Cup final")&[1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1993 UEFA Champions League final"). This was the fifth final in the history of the European Cup in which neither of the teams came from England, Germany, Italy or Spain and the first since the 1991 final when [Red Star Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Star_Belgrade "Red Star Belgrade") of Yugoslavia beat Marseille. To date, this is the last Champions League final to feature a team from outside the [Big Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Five_(association_football) "Big Five (association football)") European leagues (England, France, Germany, Italy, Spain), and the last one to be won by a team from outside those five leagues.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-2)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

### Monaco

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Monaco")]

Monaco finished second in the French [Ligue 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligue_1 "Ligue 1") the previous season, meaning that they entered the Champions League at the group stage. Monaco were placed in Group C, alongside [Deportivo La Coruña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportivo_de_La_Coru%C3%B1a "Deportivo de La Coruña"), [PSV Eindhoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSV_Eindhoven "PSV Eindhoven") and [AEK Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEK_Athens_F.C. "AEK Athens F.C."). After a 2–1 in their first win in the Netherlands and a 4–0 win at the [Stade Louis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_Louis_II "Stade Louis II") against AEK Athens, Monaco travelled to Spain, losing 1–0 by Deportivo. The Monegasque adventure really began after the return match against Deportivo, when Monaco won 8–3, which represented the highest number of goals in one match in the history of the new version of the UEFA Champions League; this record lasted until 22 November 2016, when [Legia Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legia_Warsaw "Legia Warsaw") lost 8–4 to [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"). Croatian striker [Dado Pršo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dado_Pr%C5%A1o "Dado Pršo") scored four times, while captain [Ludovic Giuly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Giuly "Ludovic Giuly") (2), [Jérôme Rothen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A9r%C3%B4me_Rothen "Jérôme Rothen"), [Jaroslav Plašil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaroslav_Pla%C5%A1il "Jaroslav Plašil") and [Édouard Cissé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Ciss%C3%A9 "Édouard Cissé") pulverised the Spanish defensive line. After two more draws against PSV and AEK Athens, Monaco finished at the top of Group C.

The first knockout round saw Monaco winning against [Lokomotiv Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Lokomotiv_Moscow "FC Lokomotiv Moscow") after a 2–1 defeat in Russia and a win 1–0 at Stade Louis II. In the quarter-finals, Monaco played [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF"). After a 4–2 loss in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") (where [Fernando Morientes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Morientes "Fernando Morientes") scored, and was applauded by his former fans), Monaco created a sensation by defeating the Spanish 3–1 at home. Monaco played against [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") in the semi-finals, and despite the exclusion of [Akis Zikos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akis_Zikos "Akis Zikos"), Monaco found enough strength to score twice and win the game 3–1.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-3) The last goal was scored by striker [Shabani Nonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabani_Nonda "Shabani Nonda"), who just returned from a seven-month injury. The second leg at [Stamford Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamford_Bridge_(stadium) "Stamford Bridge (stadium)") saw Monaco resisting Chelsea's strikes, for a final score of 2–2 to reach the European Cup final for the first time in their history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bbcsport-4)

### Porto

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Porto")]

Porto, winners of the [Primeira Liga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primeira_Liga "Primeira Liga"), [Taça de Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C3%A7a_de_Portugal "Taça de Portugal") and [UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") in 2002–03, were the only Portuguese team in the group stage, after the elimination of [Benfica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S.L._Benfica "S.L. Benfica") in the third qualifying round by Italian side [Lazio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Lazio "SS Lazio"). Porto was drawn in Group F, along with Real Madrid, [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_de_Marseille "Olympique de Marseille") and [Partizan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK_Partizan "FK Partizan"). Porto's first match was at [Partizan Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partizan_Stadium "Partizan Stadium") in [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade"). [Costinha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costinha "Costinha") scored the opening goal on 22 minutes, but [Andrija Delibašić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrija_Deliba%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Andrija Delibašić") scored the equaliser on 54 minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-5) The next match, the first at the [Estádio das Antas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A1dio_das_Antas "Estádio das Antas"), was a 3–1 loss to Real Madrid. Costinha scored the opening goal again, on seven minutes. [Iván Helguera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iv%C3%A1n_Helguera "Iván Helguera") equalised on 28 minutes; [Santiago Solari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Solari "Santiago Solari") on 37 minutes and [Zinedine Zidane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinedine_Zidane "Zinedine Zidane") on 67 scored Real Madrid's winning goals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-6)

Two straight wins against Marseille followed by a win at home against Partizan secured Porto's place in the first knockout round before the last match of the group stage, a draw in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-7) In the first knockout round, Porto met [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C."). The Portuguese won 2–1 at home[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-8) and managed to qualify in the final minutes of the second leg, when Costinha scored an equaliser in [injury time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football#Duration_and_tie-breaking_methods "Association football") in a 1–1 draw at [Old Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Trafford "Old Trafford").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-9) In the quarter-finals, Porto met a French team for the second time in the tournament: a 2–0 win at home[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-10) and a 2–2 draw in France eliminated [Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_Lyonnais "Olympique Lyonnais") from the competition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-11) In the semi-finals, Porto played Deportivo La Coruña, eliminating them 1–0 on aggregate.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-12)

## Match

### Summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Summary")]

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/FCP-CL_Supporters.jpg/250px-FCP-CL_Supporters.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FCP-CL_Supporters.jpg)

FC Porto supporters at the Gelsenkirchen Arena AufSchalke.

Monaco, in their first European final since the 1992 Europa Cup,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bbcsport-4) were up against Porto, the UEFA Cup winners from the previous season,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bbcsport-4) who were appearing in the European Cup final for a second time, after defeating [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") in the [1987 European Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_European_Cup_final "1987 European Cup final").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-uefareport-13) Porto were the favourites after eliminating Manchester United and Deportivo La Coruña in the knockout phase, while Monaco had eliminated Real Madrid and Chelsea.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Porto won the match 3–0; [Carlos Alberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Alberto_(footballer,_born_December_1984) "Carlos Alberto (footballer, born December 1984)") opened the scoring in the first half, while [Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deco "Deco") and [Dmitri Alenichev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Alenichev "Dmitri Alenichev") extended Porto's lead in the second half.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-14)
